analysis.one_liner: Outlaws most private handgun ownership, allowing possession only by police, licensed clubs, and guard services.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 1992 with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime for anyone who is not a licensed importer, manufacturer, or dealer to own or possess a handgun, with a 180-day grace period. Narrow exceptions would remain for police and government agencies, members of licensed target-shooting clubs on club premises, armed guards on the job, people who document a specific threat to their life, and antiques. Current owners who turned in their handguns during the grace period would be paid fair market value, and dealers could only sell handguns to other licensees.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities affected by handgun violence, since civilian handgun possession would largely end outside police, licensed clubs, guard services, and documented-threat exceptions. People who wanted to turn in a handgun would be paid its fair market value, though only if Congress appropriated the money.

how_it_helps.text: It would bar anyone who is not a federally licensed importer, manufacturer, or dealer from importing, transferring, transporting, or manufacturing a handgun, and from owning or possessing one after a 180-day grace period [S2] [S3].
It would require handgun sales to occur only between licensees, on licensed premises, with the buyer presenting a license, closing off private sales [S2] [S3].

It would create a narrow exception allowing a person to possess a handgun for 180 days if a local chief law enforcement officer issues a written statement that the person or a household member faces a threat to their life [S2] [S3].
It would pay fair market value to any person who lawfully acquired a handgun and surrenders it to law enforcement during the 180-day grace period [S2] [S3].
It would require owners to report a lost or stolen handgun by the end of the business day it is discovered, making it harder for diverted guns to disappear into an untraceable market [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Handgun owners, who would have to surrender, sell to a licensee, or qualify for an exception within 180 days; handgun and ammunition manufacturers and dealers, who would lose nearly the entire civilian market; and taxpayers, who would fund the fair-market-value buyback, which is effective only if money is appropriated.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners, the firearms industry, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Tens of millions of lawfully owned handguns would become unlawful to possess after 180 days, and the bill's compensation applies only to handguns surrendered during that grace period, so owners who missed the window or kept a gun for an unlisted purpose would face up to five years in prison and a $5,000 fine [S3].
The buyback payments are binding only to the extent Congress provides money in advance through appropriations, so owners could be required to surrender handguns without guaranteed compensation [S3].
The exception for people facing documented threats depends on the discretion of a local chief law enforcement officer, so protection would vary by where a person lives [S3].

Most critics and many gun owners regarded a near-total civilian handgun ban as beyond what the Constitution allows and far broader than public opinion would accept; the bill attracted no cosponsors, including from the sponsor's own party, which is general knowledge not found in the provided sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A near-total civilian handgun ban would be one of the most sweeping firearms restrictions ever proposed in Congress, with a real potential to reduce handgun deaths and trafficking. But the costs are equally real: it would disarm tens of millions of lawful owners, compensation is not guaranteed, and it goes well beyond the background-check and waiting-period measures that have historically drawn broader support. The complete absence of cosponsors suggests even gun-control supporters in Congress viewed this design as too extreme to advance.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1992, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, cosponsors, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Solarz, a New York Democrat, introduced the Handgun Control Act of 1992 on August 12, 1992 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day, and on August 25, 1992 to its Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill had zero cosponsors and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Handgun owners and the firearms industry, which keeps its civilian market; the bill died without anyone having to vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

for.name: Rep. Stephen J. Solarz
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill imposing strict federal controls on handgun ownership and possession.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred, through its Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its crime subcommittee on August 25, 1992 and never held a hearing or markup, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House members of both parties
against.what_they_did: Not one member, including fellow Democrats, signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's nearly five months of existence.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only signal is that the Democratic sponsor drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan alignment can be measured.

industries.note: The bill bans civilian import, manufacture, and transfer of handguns and bars anyone from making firearms or ammunition for sale without a dealer's license, eliminating the civilian market. Manufacturers' interest in the bill ran against the public-safety purpose its sponsor described [S2] [S3].

Dealers could only sell handguns to other licensees on licensed premises, ending retail handgun sales to the public. Their existing business would be largely eliminated rather than regulated [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Licensed pistol clubs and armed guard services
industries.note: These are the only private entities that could keep handguns under the bill, via a new federal licensing system with recordkeeping and inspection requirements. The bill locks in their exclusive licensed role while imposing new costs and oversight on them [S2] [S3].
Police and government agencies are fully exempt, and licensed guard services keep a protected role. Surrendered handguns and buyback payments would flow through law enforcement agencies [S2] [S3].
